title: How long will you wait?
hookLine: you're not a child anymore, and Socrates became himself by attending to reason in everything (Enchiridion 51)

lines: MONDAY. THE FIRST OF THE MONTH.
cards: Monday. That's when it starts. Or the first of the month.
Or after the holidays, after this project, after the kids are older, after things calm down. There's a thing you're going to begin, and a date it's going to begin on, and the date keeps moving.
Near the very end of the handbook, Epictetus stops giving rules and turns to his student with a question, aimed straight at that moving date.

teach.h: WHAT TEACHER ARE YOU WAITING FOR?
teach.b: How long will you put off thinking yourself worthy of the best things, he asks, and never crossing what reason tells you? You've received the principles you ought to accept. You've accepted them.
So what teacher are you still waiting for, before you start setting yourself right?
You're not a boy any longer, he says. You're a grown adult.

If you keep being careless and lazy, adding delay to delay, setting one day and then another for when you'll start paying attention to yourself, you'll fail to notice you're not making progress, and you'll live and die an ordinary person.
So whenever something hard or pleasant, glorious or shameful, comes along, remember: the contest is now. The Olympic games are here. They can't be put off.
Progress is saved or lost by a single defeat, a single giving way. The Greek word for contest is agōn, the word for the games.
This, Epictetus says, is how Socrates became who he was: by paying attention to nothing but reason in everything he met.

teach.h: LIVE AS ONE WHO WANTS TO BE SOCRATES.
teach.b: And you, even if you're not yet Socrates, should live as someone who wants to be.
The week closes here, and every line in it could start today: doesn't follow, quickly, not badly, show the wool, in secret, blame no one, live the book.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism return to Enchiridion 51 when they notice themselves postponing something important, and take one small step that same day.

o: the contest, which is happening now, not later
a long training season before the real test
the pain you feel when progress is slow

games.q: how long will you wait — tap the pairs.
p: what teacher are you waiting for?

s: Epictetus says you must become Socrates before you start
even if you're not yet Socrates, live as someone who wants to be.
he compares the moment of choice to the Olympic games
the contest is now, and it can't be put off.

games.q: you've meant to start for months, and Monday is three days away. what does Enchiridion 51 say?
o: wait for Monday. a clean start is better.
the contest is now. start today.
wait for a better teacher first.
games.why: what teacher are you waiting for? the games are here and can't be put off. progress is saved or lost by a single giving way.

practice: Name the thing you've been meaning to start, the call, the practice, the apology, the first page, and the date you keep giving it: Monday, next month, someday. Ask Epictetus' question, kindly but honestly: how long will you wait?
Then find the smallest first step, so small there's no reason to postpone it, and picture taking it.

wordCard.voice: Agōn. The Greek word for a contest, the games that can't be put off; you're grown, and the contest is now. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a contest or struggle. In Enchiridion 51, the contest is now.

carryVoice: Your line: the contest is now. The games are here, and they don't wait for Monday. Day three hundred eighty-five, and a week done.
